{"id": "19978836-40a6-40e7-a55a-cf20fde523b3", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Short answer: almost certainly not a failed optimization — what you're likely seeing is a reporting-lag and attribution artifact in how the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT) accounts for usage, not a real increase from moving cold data to Deep Archive.

A few things to know about how the tool works, verified against AWS docs:

- **Monthly data with a lag**: CCFT emissions are published monthly, typically between the 15th–21st of the *following* month. If the 40 TB migration happened late in a quarter, the one-time transfer activity and the new Deep Archive storage may land in different reporting periods than you'd expect, making a single quarter's total misleading on its own.
- **Migration itself has a footprint, separate from storage**: Reading 40 TB out of S3 Standard and writing it into Glacier Deep Archive generates request and data-transfer activity. That's accounted for as its own usage in the period the migration ran — it's a one-time bump layered on top of (not instead of) the storage emissions, so the quarter you migrated in can look worse even though it sets up a long-term win.
- **Service-level aggregation can mask the win**: CCFT reports roll up at the service level (e.g., "S3" overall), not broken out per storage class. If other S3 usage grew in the same quarter — more Standard storage elsewhere, more requests, more replicated data — that growth can outweigh the drop from this one migration in the total you're looking at.
- **Deep Archive's steady-state emissions are lower**, so the benefit should show up as a declining trend in subsequent months once the one-time migration overhead rolls off — it just won't show up as an instant drop in the same quarter.

What I'd check before concluding anything failed:
1. Look at the month-over-month trend for the 2–3 months *after* the migration, not just the single quarter it happened in.
2. Pull the finer-grained view via AWS Data Exports (1-gram CO2e resolution) rather than the dashboard's 1 kg resolution — the dashboard can round small shifts to zero or obscure them.
3. Isolate S3 request/transfer emissions from S3 storage emissions for that period if your export has that breakdown, so the one-time migration cost doesn't get conflated with ongoing storage cost.

If you want, I can help you frame this as a recommendation to track or pull together a report comparing your pre- and post-migration months once you have the finer-grained data.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
